abstract: The clinical-stage drug PRLX-93936 acts as a molecular glue that reprograms TRIM21 to degrade nuclear pore proteins, establishing a therapeutic mechanism that drives apoptosis in pancreatic cancer.
methods:
Methods
Cell Lines
PANC-1 (cat. # CRL-1469, RRID:CVCL_0480), Panc 08.13 (cat. # CRL-2551, RRID:CVCL_1638), Panc 02.03 (cat. # CRL-2553, RRID:CVCL_1633), AsPC-1 cells (cat. # CRL-1682, RRID:CVCL_0152), and hTERT RPE-1 (cat. # CRL-4000, RRID:CVCL_4388) were purchased from the ATCC. HEK293T (RRID:CVCL_0063), KP-3 (RRID:CVCL_3005), Hs 766T (RRID:CVCL_0334), LS 180 (RRID:CVCL_0397), SK-MES-1 (RRID:CVCL_0630), CAL 33 (RRID:CVCL_1108), CAL 27 (RRID:CVCL_1107), LN-18 (RRID:CVCL_0392), Kuramochi (RRID:CVCL_1345), UACC-257 (RRID:CVCL_1779), and NCI-H661 (RRID:CVCL_1577) cell lines were obtained from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia. PANC-1 cells expressing nuclear-localized mKate2 were a gift from S.J. Dixon. PANC-1, Hs 766T, SK-MES-1, CAL 33, CAL 27, LN-18, and HEK293T cells were cultured in DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific), with 10% heat-inactivated FBS (Sigma-Aldrich) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific). AsPC-1, KP-3, Kuramochi, UACC-257, and H661 cells were cultured in RPMI (Thermo Fisher Scientific), with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Panc 08.13 cells were cultured in RPMI medium, with 15% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin, 2 mmol/L glutamine, 1 mmol/L sodium pyruvate, 60 μg/mL insulin, 10 mmol/L HEPES, 1.5 g/L sodium bicarbonate, and 4.5 g/L glucose. Panc 02.03 cells were cultured in RPMI medium with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin, and 1 mmol/L sodium pyruvate. LS 180 cells were cultured in minimum essential medium, with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. All cell lines were grown in humidified tissue culture incubators at 37°C with 5% CO
2
, were
mycoplasma
-negative by MycoAlert (Lonza) and/or MycoStrip (InvivoGen), and were authenticated by short tandem repeat fingerprinting (Labcorp) using the PowerPlex 16 HS assay (Promega).
Patient-Derived Pancreatic Cancer Organoids
Processed HCMI organoid RNA-seq data were downloaded from the NCI HCMI web portal (
www.cancer.gov/ccg/research/functional-genomics/hcmi
; Database of Genotypes and Phenotypes (dbGaP) accession number phs001486). HCM-BROD-0019-C25 (cat. # PDM-166), HCM-CSHL-0092-C25 (cat. # PDM-39), HCM-CSHL-0080-C25 (cat. # PDM-31), HCM-CSHL-0079-C25 (cat. # PDM-30), HCM-CSHL-0078-C25 (cat. # PDM-29), HCM-CSHL-0509-C24 (cat. # PDM-445), and HCM-BROD-0110-C25 (cat. # PDM-134) were purchased from the ATCC. Organoids were cultured in 50% advanced DMEM/F-12 (Invitrogen) and 50% L-WRN conditioned media from L-WRN (Wnt-3A, R-spondin 3, and noggin conditioned medium), supplemented with 1% penicillin–streptomycin, 1 mmol/L HEPES, 1 × GlutaMAX, 1 × B27 supplement minus vitamin A (Invitrogen, cat. #12587001), 50 ng/mL human EGF (Invitrogen, cat. #AF-100-15-100UG), 100 ng/mL human FGF10 (BioLegend, cat. # 559304), 10 nmol/L human gastrin I (Bio-Techne, cat. #3006), 1 mmol/L N-acetyl cysteine (Sigma, cat. # A9165), 10 mmol/L nicotinamide (Sigma, cat. # N0636), 0.5 μmol/L A83-01 (Cayman Chemical, cat. # 9001799), 10 μmol/L SB202190 (Cayman Chemical, cat. # 10010399), and 100 μg/mL Normocin (InvivoGen, cat. # ant-nr-1). Cells in Cultrex basement membrane (Bio-Techne, cat. # 3533-010-02) were plated as 40 μL droplets in 24-well plates and treated with complete organoid media supplemented with 10 μmol/L CHIR 99021 (Cayman Chemical, cat. # 13122) and 10 μmol/L Y-27632 (Cayman Chemical, cat. #10005583) after the droplets had solidified for 15 minutes at 37°C. The medium was refreshed every 3 to 4 days, and organoids were passaged every 2 to 4 weeks by enzymatic dissociation with TrypLE (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All cells were grown in humidified tissue culture incubators at 37°C with 5% CO
2
and were confirmed to be mycoplasma-negative by MycoAlert (Lonza).
Cell Viability Assays
For cell line viability assays, cells were seeded at a density of 1,000 cells per well in 384-well flat-bottom white TC-treated microplates (Corning). The following day, cells were treated with a serial dilution of test compounds using the D300e digital dispenser (Tecan). After 72 hours of incubation, cell viability was assessed by the CellTiter-Glo luminescent cell viability assay (Promega). Luminescence was measured using a PHERAstar FSX plate reader (BMG Labtech). Data were baseline-corrected by normalizing to the DMSO control. Dose–response curves were generated using Prism 10 (GraphPad), and IC
50
values were calculated accordingly.
For organoid assays, organoids were dissociated into single cells and seeded at a density of 1,500 cells per well in 5% Cultrex in 384-well flat-bottom microplates using a published approach (
60
). The following day, cells were treated with a serial dilution of compounds using the D300e digital dispenser. After 5 days of incubation, viability was quantified using the CellTiter-Glo assay, as described above.
PRISM Screening
The PRISM cell proliferation assay was carried out as previously described (
21
). In brief, approximately 900 barcoded cell lines in pools of 20 to 25 were thawed and plated into 384-well plates (1,250 cells per well for adherent cells, 2,000 cells per well for suspension or mixed suspension–adherent pools). Cells were treated with an eight-point compound dose curve starting at 10 μmol/L with 3-fold dilutions in triplicate and incubated for 120 hours. Following lysis, the barcode for each cell line was read out by mRNA-based Luminex detection and processed using a standardized R pipeline (
https://github.com/broadinstitute/prism_data_processing
) to generate viability estimates relative to vehicle treatment and dose–response metrics. The AUC was used as a metric of drug potency for each cell line. Reference publicly available gene expression data were retrieved from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (
61
). Predictive biomarker relationships were determined by comparing each cell line’s baseline molecular feature (e.g., RNA-seq gene expression) with the observed AUC models by univariate linear modeling available on the Cancer Dependency Map website (
34
).
Transfection and Lentivirus Production
HEK293T cells were seeded at a density of 35,000 per well in 1 mL of DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. The following day, a packaging mix was prepared by combining 800 ng psPAX2, 300 ng pMD2.G, and 900 ng sgRNA backbone in 125 μL OptiMEM (Invitrogen). This mixture was then combined with 6 μL TransIT-LT1 (Mirus Bio) in 125 μL OptiMEM, incubated for 25 minutes at room temperature, and then added dropwise to the cells. After 2 days, the medium containing lentivirus was collected and stored at −80°C before use. To transduce target cells, the lentivirus was added to the cells in the presence of 1 mg/mL polybrene.
CRISPR KO of Target Genes
sgRNAs targeting
TRIM21
were designed utilizing the Broad Institute CRISPick design tool (
62
). Five pairs of oligonucleotides (IDT) targeting
TRIM21
and a control pair targeting an intergenic region (CHR2-2) were annealed and cloned into the pXPR_023 vector. In brief, the vector was linearized using BsmBI (New England Biolabs). The annealed oligonucleotides were then ligated into the linearized and purified vector backbone with T4 DNA ligase (New England Biolabs). Constructs were transformed into competent cells, purified using the Miniprep Kit (QIAGEN), and verified through Sanger sequencing to confirm the guide sequence. PANC-1 cells were stably transduced with lentivirus containing either
TRIM21
pXPR_023 or CHR2-2 pXPR_023 in 12-well plates via centrifugation at 2,000 rpm and 30°C. The following day, cells were split into flasks and selected with 2 μg/mL puromycin for 3 days. Seven days after transduction, genomic DNA (gDNA) of transduced cells was extracted, and PCRs were performed to amplify ∼200 base pairs flanking the edited site, followed by NGS sequencing to evaluate the efficacy. A similar workflow was used for other sgRNAs targeting
IRF2
,
CHUK
,
IKBKG
,
HCFC2
, and
NUP98
.
Gene Overexpression
The
TRIM21
cDNA (Addgene, 116941; gift from Gaudenz Danuser) was cloned into the pDONR221 vector (cat. # 12536017, Thermo Fisher Scientific) using BP Clonase (cat. # 11891020, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and then transferred to the pLX_311 vector using LR Clonase (cat. # 11791020, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Lentivirus was generated as described above. Cell lines were infected with the harvested lentivirus, and infected cells were selected with 2 mg/mL blasticidin (cat. # A1113903, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 10 days.
PANC-1 CRISPR-Cas9 Genome-Wide KO Screen
PANC-1 cells were stably transduced with pLX_311-Cas9. The Brunello genome-scale sgRNA library was obtained from the Broad Institute Genetic Perturbation Platform (GPP) (
63
). Virus was titrated to achieve a goal infection efficiency of 30% to 50%. PANC-1–Cas9 cells were infected in 12-well plates via centrifugation at 2,000 rpm and 30°C for 2 hours. The following day, cells were split into two replicate flasks and selected with 2 μg/mL puromycin for 5 days. After selection, replicates were seeded into 110 nmol/L PRLX or DMSO control. Cells were maintained at 37°C and 5% CO
2
in CellSTACK 1,272 cm
2
2-stack flasks (Corning) in RPMI with 10% FBS. Cells were reseeded every ∼3 days at a minimum of 40 million cells per passage to maintain ∼500× library representation. Media and drugs were refreshed every 3 to 4 days for a total of 3 weeks. Drug concentration was gradually escalated to a final concentration of 250 nmol/L PRLX or 5 μmol/L erastin. gDNA was isolated from cell pellets using the NucleoSpin Blood XL columns (MACHEREY-NAGEL). gDNA PCR and next-generation sequencing by standard Illumina methods were performed to determine guide abundance.
PANC-1 CRISPR-dCas9 Genome-Wide Activation Screen
PANC-1 cells were stably transduced with pXPR_109 to express dCas9-VP64. The Calabrese B genome-scale virus library was obtained from the GPP (
63
). PANC-1–dCas9-VP64 cells were infected with this library via centrifugation as described earlier. The following day, cells were split into two replicates and reseeded. One day later, 2 μg/mL of puromycin was added. After selection for 5 days, replicates were split into DMSO or 110 nmol/L PRLX drug arms in duplicate and cultured for 2 weeks as described, followed by gDNA isolation and sequencing (both as described earlier).
CRISPR Screen Analysis
Guides targeting multiple genes or with few reads in the plasmid DNA pool were filtered. Counts were normalized against total library size. The guide-level log
2
fold change was computed using the ratio between treatment and vehicle control counts. The median log
2
fold change from all guides targeting each gene was calculated. Statistical significance for each gene-level result was calculated using the MAGeCK-RRA method (MAGeCK version 0.5.9.5), using 10,000 permutations. Two-sided
P
values were corrected for multiple hypothesis testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg method.
TRIM21 Base Editor Tiled Library Preparation
Guide sequences were designed against NGN protospacer adjacent motif sites across the TRIM21 coding sequence (ENST00000254436.8) using the Broad Institute GPP Beagle Tool, extending up to two bases into each intron (
64
). In total, we included 752 sgRNAs targeting the TRIM21 coding sequence, 30 sgRNAs targeting 30 essential genes, and 100 nontargeting sgRNAs. The oligonucleotide pool was synthesized by Genscript and subsequently PCR amplified (forward primer, 5′-3′ was GTGTAACCCGTAGGG
CACCT
; reverse primer, 5′-3′ was
GTCGA
GAGCAGTCCTTCGAC). Using Golden Gate cloning with Esp3I (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and T7 ligase (New England Biolabs), amplicons were cloned into pRDA_478 (SpG-BE3max) and pRDA_479 (SpG-ABE8e). The ligation product was isopropanol precipitated and electroporated into Endura electrocompetent cells (Biosearch Technologies) and grown at 37°C for 16 hours on agar plates with 100 μg/mL carbenicillin. Colonies were scraped, and plasmid DNA was harvested (EndoFree Plasmid Maxi, QIAGEN).
Lentivirus Production, Lentiviral Titer, and Small Molecules for Base Editor Screen
For virus production, we followed the protocol previously described (
64
). In brief, PANC-1 cells were infected with a viral volume resulting in 30% to 50% transduction efficiency. Puromycin (2 μg/mL) was added 2 days after transduction and maintained for 5 to 7 days to ensure complete depletion of nontransduced cells. Upon puromycin removal, cells were split into drug arms (each at a representation of at least 1,000 coverage per sgRNA) and passaged every 2 to 4 days for an additional 2 weeks to allow sgRNAs to be enriched or depleted; cell counts were taken at each passage to monitor growth. PRLX (Cayman Chemical) was screened at 110 nmol/L, escalated to 150 nmol/L, and JWZ-8-103 was screened at 15 nmol/L, escalated to 20 nmol/L. DMSO alone was used as the vehicle.
gDNA Isolation, Sequencing, and Base Editing Analysis
gDNA was isolated using the NucleoSpin Blood gDNA kit (MACHEREY-NAGEL). The gDNA concentrations were quantitated by the DNA Broad Range Assay (DeNovix). gDNA was processed prior to PCR using the OneStep PCR Inhibitor Removal Kit (Zymo). For PCR amplification, 10 μg of gDNA or 100 pg of library plasmid DNA in a final reaction volume of 100 μL per well was used in a 96-well plate, as previously described (
64
). Pooled PCR products were purified with Agencourt AMPure XP SPRI beads according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Beckman Coulter, A63880). Illumina sequencing was performed by Novogene. Guide sequences were extracted from sequencing reads using the Broad PoolQ script. Compound-treated conditions were compared with the time-matched vehicle controls to calculate the log
2
fold change and
z
-score values for each guide. For amino acid analyses, corresponding adenines or cytosines in positions 4 to 8 of the sgRNA (in which positions 21–23 are the protospacer adjacent motif adjacent to the sgRNA) were considered to be edited. We next used this information to annotate each sgRNA with its predicted amino acid changes. We ordered the mutation types as follows: nonsense > splice site > missense > intron > silent > untranslated region, as previously reported (
65
). Guides containing multiple mutation types were considered the most severe mutation type. For the display item showing base editor hits mapped onto the predicted TRIM21 structure, we used AlphaFold 3 (
66
) to generate a model of the TRIM21 dimer, using as inputs the following UniProt entities:
P19474
(TRIM21),
P61088
(UBE2N), and
P62068
(ubiquitin). We also included four Zn atoms. The top model was taken for display. We used the specified base editor–predicted mutated residues according to the cutoff shown (
z
-score >4, adenine base editor data, 6 days) and displayed these residues as yellow spheres (carbons). We manually removed base editor hits that made internal hydrophobic contacts in globular domains for clarity, as these are predicted to create null alleles by fully disrupting TRIM21 folding.
Quantitative Global Proteome Profiling via LC/MS-MS
WT or TRIM21 KO PANC-1 cells were seeded the day prior and treated with DMSO or the indicated compounds across 3 to 4 biological replicates for various time points. WT or NUP98 sgRNA3–expressing PANC-1 cells were treated with DMSO or PRLX (1 μmol/L) for 7 days. After treatment, cells were detached using trypsin, neutralized with media, and washed twice with either TBS [50 mmol/L Tris (pH 8.5) and 150 mmol/L NaCl] or PBS. The treated and washed cell pellets were stored at −80°C until further use. Lysis was performed by first thermally denaturing the samples in residual wash buffer for 5 minutes at 95°C. Fresh lysis buffer [8 mol/L urea, 150 mmol/L NaCl, and 100 mmol/L HEPES (pH 8.0) in MS-grade water] was then added, and the lysates were homogenized using needle ultrasonication. Protein concentrations were measured via a Bradford protein concentration assay (Bio-Rad, 5000006), and the samples were normalized to 30 μg of 2 mg/mL by diluting with lysis buffer. The samples were then reduced and alkylated simultaneously by adding final concentrations of freshly prepared 10 mmol/L Tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine hydrochloride (TCEP; Sigma-Aldrich, C4706) and 40 mmol/L chloroacetamide (Sigma-Aldrich, C0267) in 100 mmol/L HEPES, pH 8.0, and shaking for 30 to 60 minutes. The samples were then diluted by the addition of CaCl
2
(Sigma-Aldrich, C4901) in 50 mmol/L HEPES, pH 8.0, to final concentrations of ∼1 mol/L urea and 1 mmol/L CaCl
2
. Digestion using a 1:100 (w/w) ratio of protease to protein lysate with MS-grade Trypsin/Lys-C Protease Mix (Thermo A40009) was then performed by mixing overnight at 37°C. The samples were then acidified by adding trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) until the sample pH was ≤3, as confirmed by pH paper. Samples were then desalted using SOLAμ SPE HRP Peptide Desalting columns (Thermo 60209-001) with a Positive Pressure Manifold and all MS-grade reagents. The desalting cartridges were activated with 200 μL of acetonitrile and then equilibrated with two washes of 200 μL Wash Buffer (2% acetonitrile + 0.2% TFA in water). After loading samples into the cartridges, the samples were washed 3 times with 200 μL wash buffer and then eluted using 100 μL of 50% acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid (FA) in water. The desalted peptides were then immediately dried on a centrifugal vacuum concentrator (Thermo SPD120-115). The samples were then reconstituted in 0.1% FA in water and analyzed by LC/MS-MS (see section below).
Ubiquitylation Proteomics
PANC-1 cells were seeded and treated the following day with DMSO or 1 μmol/L MG132 for 1 hour, followed by the addition of DMSO or 500 nmol/L PRLX for 30 minutes. Cells were detached using trypsin, which was neutralized with media, and then washed twice with TBS (50 mmol/L Tris, pH 8.5, and 150 mmol/L NaCl). Lysis was performed by first thermally denaturing the samples in residual wash buffer for 5 minutes at 95°C. Fresh Lysis Buffer (8 mol/L urea, 150 mmol/L NaCl, and 100 mmol/L HEPES, pH 8.0, in MS-grade water) was then added, and the lysates were homogenized using needle ultrasonication and then normalized to 6.6 mg of 5 mg/mL by diluting with Lysis Buffer via a Bradford protein concentration assay (Bio-Rad 5000006). The samples were then reduced and alkylated simultaneously by adding final concentrations of freshly prepared 10 mmol/L tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine hydrochloride (TCEP; Sigma-Aldrich, C4706) and 40 mmol/L chloroacetamide (Sigma-Aldrich, C0267) in 100 mmol/L HEPES (pH 8.0) and shaking for 30 to 60 minutes. The samples were then diluted by the addition of CaCl
2
(Sigma-Aldrich, C4901) in 50 mmol/L HEPES (pH 8.0) for final concentrations of ∼2 mol/L urea and 1 mmol/L CaCl
2
. Digestion using a 1:100 (w/w) protease–to–protein lysate ratio with MS-grade Trypsin/Lys-C Protease Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A40009) was then performed by mixing overnight at 37°C. The digested peptides were acidified using 1/20th the volume of 20% TFA for a final concentration of 1% TFA, clarified by centrifugation at 1,780 ×
g
at room temperature for 15 minutes, and then desalted using C18 desalting columns (Cell Signaling Technology PTMScan Peptide Purification Kit #35741) following the manufacturer’s protocol. A small fraction of the eluted desalted peptides (∼4 μg) was reserved, dried separately by a centrifugal vacuum concentrator (Thermo Fisher Scientific, SPD120-115), and injected into the LC/MS-MS for whole-proteome analysis to assess digestion quality and monitor possible protein level changes in the samples. The remaining eluted desalted peptides were frozen in a dry ice and ethanol bath and then thoroughly dried by lyophilization to maximize the removal of residual TFA in the sample.
Ubiquitylated peptides containing the diglycine remnant following trypsin digestion were subsequently enriched using immunoaffinity purification with the PTMScan Ubiquitin Remnant Motif (K-ε-GG) Kit (#5562, Cell Signaling Technology) following the kit’s procedure. The enriched ubiquitylated peptides were desalted using the same SOLAμ SPE HRP Peptide Desalting column procedure as described above, dried, and subsequently reconstituted in 0.1% FA in water and then analyzed using LC/MS-MS (see section below).
Proximity Labeling Proteomics
PANC-1 TRIM21 KO cells were stably transduced with TRIM21–TurboID or TurboID–TRIM21 fusion constructs. TRIM21 functionality was verified by assessing cell viability following compound treatment at 72 hours, as described above. For proximity labeling, cells were pretreated with 1 μmol/L MG132 for 30 minutes, followed by treatment with 0.5 μmol/L PRLX for 30 minutes, 2 hours, and 4 hours. Prior to sample collection, 100 μmol/L biotin was added for the final 30 minutes. After treatments, cell pellets were rinsed twice with PBS and lysed in RIPA lysis buffer containing 1% Triton X-100, a protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich), phosphatase inhibitor cocktail 2 (Sigma-Aldrich), and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail 3 (Sigma-Aldrich). Protein concentrations were assessed by BCA protein assay to ensure equal loading across samples. Cell lysates were incubated with Pierce streptavidin magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 4°C overnight to enrich biotinylated proteins. The beads were washed sequentially with 1 mol/L KCl, 0.1 mol/L Na
2
CO3, RIPA buffer, and TBS (50 mmol/L Tris-HCl, 150 mmol/L NaCl, pH 7.5). For Western blot analysis, the enriched proteins were eluted by boiling the beads in 1.5× protein loading buffer at 95°C for 10 minutes. For proteomics analysis, the beads were then washed twice with 200 μL of 50 mmol/L HEPES (pH 7.4) and followed by two washes with 200 μL of 2 mol/L urea in 50 mmol/L HEPES (pH 7.4) buffer to equilibrate the enriched proteins for digestion. The beads were then incubated with 80 μL of 2 mol/L urea in 50 mmol/L HEPES containing 1 mmol/L dithiothreitol and 0.4 μg Trypsin/Lys-C Protease Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A40009) at 25°C for 1 hour while shaking at 1,000 rpm. This supernatant was then transferred to fresh tubes. The streptavidin beads were then eluted twice with 60 μL of 2 mol/L urea in 50 mmol/L HEPES (pH 7.4) buffer. These two elutions were combined with the on-bead digest supernatant from before. The combined elutions were reduced using a final concentration of 4 mmol/L dithiothreitol by shaking at 25°C for 30 minutes and then alkylated using a final concentration of 10 mmol/L iodoacetamide by shaking for an additional 45 minutes at 25°C. An additional 0.5 μg Trypsin/Lys-C Protease Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A40009) was added, and the samples were digested overnight at 25°C while shaking. The digested samples were then acidified to a final concentration of 0.8% TFA and subsequently desalted using SOLAμ SPE HRP Peptide Desalting columns as described above. Samples were reconstituted in 0.1% FA in water.
LC/MS-MS diaPASEF Acquisition and Statistical Analysis
diaPASEF LC/MS-MS Analysis
The reconstituted desalted peptides were then analyzed using a nanoElute 2 ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC; Bruker Daltonics) coupled to a timsTOF HT (Bruker Daltonics) via a CaptiveSpray nano-electrospray source. The peptides were separated in the UHPLC using an Aurora Ultimate nanoflow UHPLC column with CSI fitting (25 cm × 75 μm ID, 1.7 μm C18; IonOptics, AUR3-25075C18-CSI) over a 70-minute gradient at a flow rate of 400 nL/minute, with the column temperature maintained at 50°C using mobile phase A (3% acetonitrile + 0.1% FA in water) and mobile phase B (MPB; 0.1% FA in acetonitrile). The 70-minute gradient started at 6% MPB, increasing to 17% MPB at 40 minutes, 25% MPB at 55 minutes, 34% MPB at 64 minutes, and 85% MPB at 65 minutes and finishing at 92% MPB at 70 minutes.
diaPASEF was performed using the MS settings of 100 m/z for Scan Begin and 1,700 m/z for Scan End in positive mode, the TIMS settings of 0.70 V⋅s/cm
2
for 1/K
0
start, 1.30 V⋅s/cm
2
for 1/K
0
end, a ramp time of 120.0 ms, a 100% duty cycle, a ramp rate of 7.93 Hz, and the capillary voltage set to 1,600 V. diaPASEF windows from a mass range of 226.8 to 1,226.8 Da and a mobility range of 0.70 to 1.30 1/K
0
were designed to provide 25 Da windows covering doubly and triply charged peptides, as confirmed by DDA-PASEF scans, whereas singly charged peptides were excluded from the acquisition due to their position in the m/z-ion mobility plane.
Raw Data Processing
The raw diaPASEF files were processed using library-free analysis in FragPipe 22.0 using diaTracer (
67
). Data-independent acquisition (DIA) spectrum deconvolution was performed using diaTracer 1.1.5 with the following default settings: (i) “Delta Apex IM” set to 0.01, (ii) “Delta Apex retention time” set to 3, (iii) “RF max” set to 500, (iv) “Corr threshold” set to 0.3, and (v) mass defect filter enabled with the offset set to 0.1. The reviewed
Homo sapiens
protein sequence database was obtained from UniProt (July 13, 2024; 20,468 entities) with decoys and common contaminants. In the MSFragger 4.1 database search, the following settings were used: (i) initial precursor and fragment mass tolerances of 10 and 20 ppm, respectively; (ii) enabled spectrum deisotoping, mass calibration, and parameter optimization; and (iii) isotope error set to “0/1/2.” For protein digestion, “stricttrypsin” for fully tryptic peptides was enabled with up to one missed cleavage, peptide length from 7 to 50, and peptide mass range from 500 to 5,000 Da. For modifications, methionine oxidation (two max occurrences) and N-terminal acetylation (one max occurrence) were set as variable modifications (maximum of three), whereas cysteine carbamidomethylation was set as a fixed modification. For ubiquitylation proteomics, the K-ε-GG remnant (Unimod 121) was included as a variable modification (max 2) on lysine. For validation, MSBooster (DIA-NN model) and Percolator were used for retention time and MS-MS spectra prediction and peptide-spectrum match rescoring, whereas ProteinProphet (–maxppmdiff 2000000) was used for protein inference with FDR filtering (–picked –prot 0.01). The spectral library was then generated by EasyPQP 0.1.49 using default settings. Peptides were then quantified using DIA-NN 1.9.1 with 0.1% FDR and QuantUMS high-accuracy settings. The DIA-NN parquet report containing peptide quantification and scoring was then analyzed in R.
Statistical Analysis for Global Proteome Profiling and Proximity Proteomics
DIA-NN quantified peptides were then further filtered, including (i) common contaminants and reverse sequences, (ii) 1% FDR filtering at the global.q.value (precursor Q value across all samples) and pg.q.value (protein group
Q
value in a single injection), (iii) quantification of a given peptide in at least two replicates in one condition, and (iv) removal of singly charged peptides and nonproteotypic (unique) peptides. Protein intensities were then recalculated using the MaxLFQ method (
68
) provided in the DIA-NN R package. Differential statistics was then performed using the DEqMS (
69
) R package, which performs a LIMMA-moderated
t
test with an adjustment for the number of detected peptides per protein, to determine the
P
value, fold change, and Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted
P
value.
Statistical Analysis for Ubiquitylation Proteomics
DIA-NN quantified peptides were then further filtered, including (i) common contaminants and reverse sequences, (ii) 1% FDR filtering at the global.q.value (precursor
Q
value across all samples), (iii) quantification of a given peptide in at least two replicates in one condition, and (iv) removal of singly charged peptides and nonproteotypic (unique) peptides. MaxLFQ intensities were then calculated for ubiquitylated peptides by their assigned ubiquitylation site within the human proteome using the DIA-NN R package. Differential statistics was then performed using the DEqMS R package, which performs a LIMMA-moderated
t
test with an adjustment for the number of detected peptides per ubiquitylation site, to determine the
P
value, fold change, and Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted
P
value.
Cellular Thermal Shift Assay
PANC-1 cell pellets were harvested and washed twice with PBS and then suspended in PBS containing a protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma P8340), phosphatase inhibitor cocktail 2 (Sigma-Aldrich, P5726), and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail 3 (Sigma-Aldrich, P0044). The cells were lysed by repeating three freeze-thaw cycles using liquid N
2
. The lysates were centrifuged at 20,000
g
for 5 minutes at 25°C, and then the supernatants were collected and divided into three aliquots, with two aliquots treated with JWZ-8-103 and the third aliquot treated with DMSO as a control by coincubation at 37°C for 1 hour. Each treated mixture was subsequently divided into 12 aliquots of 40 μL in PCR tubes. Thermal cycling was performed using a Veriti 96-well instrument (Applied Biosystems) with a 12-temperature gradient protocol, with each step lasting 3 minutes, followed by an additional 3 minutes of incubation at 25°C. After thermal cycling, the lysates were centrifuged at 20,000
g
for 40 minutes at 4°C. Supernatants were collected, and 40 μL of each sample was mixed with 2 μL of β-mercaptoethanol and 10 μL of SDS sample loading buffer. The mixtures were vortexed thoroughly and incubated at 25°C for 45 minutes before loading onto a gel for further analysis.
Systematic Quantification of Population Cell Death Kinetics in PANC-1 Cell Culture
The STACK assay was used to quantify drug-induced cell death in PANC-1 cells. A total of 1,500 cells expressing a nucleus-localizing fluorescent mKate2 were seeded in 50 μL into each well of a 384-well tissue culture plate (Corning, #3764). The plate was briefly spun (500 rpm, 2 seconds) to evenly settle the cells and remove bubbles. The cells were then allowed to adhere overnight. The PK study was performed in the Drug Metabolism and Pharmacokinetics (DMPK) Core facility at Scripps Florida. PKs were tested in male C57BL/6 mice via intravenous dosing in the tail vein, i.p. injection, and oral gavage. Triplicate mice were dosed at 1 mg/kg intravenously, 3 mg/kg intraperitoneally, and 6 mg/kg orally, formulated at 0.2 mg/mL (intravenously), 0.3 mg/mL (intraperitoneally), and 0.6 mg/mL (orally) in a 5:5:90 DMSO/Tween80/water solution. Approximately 20 μL of blood was collected after 5, 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 360, and 480 minutes. We used a microsampling technique in which blood is collected in capillary hematocrit tubes to reduce the total blood taken from the mouse. This allowed a single mouse to be used for the entire time course and reduced interindividual variability. Additionally, by using small sample volumes, the health of the mouse is maintained. Plasma was generated by standard centrifugation techniques, yielding approximately 10 μL of plasma, which was immediately frozen. Plasma (5 μL) was treated with 75 μL of an 80:20 acetonitrile/water solution containing 20 ng/mL carbamazepine as an internal standard and allowed to sit on ice for approximately 30 minutes to precipitate plasma proteins. A standard curve ranging from 1 to 3,300 ng/mL was prepared in mouse plasma and processed with the samples. Samples were filtered through a 0.2-micron filter and directly analyzed. Drug concentrations were determined by mass spectrometry using an SCIEX 5500 mass spectrometer with multiple reaction monitoring, using the mass transition of 365.2 to 99 for PRLX and 418.2 to 99 for JWZ-8-103, and comparing the peak area with the area of the carbamazepine internal standard. PK parameters were calculated using a noncompartmental model (Phoenix WinNonlin, Pharsight Inc.). Mice received 200 μL containing vehicle, PRLX (50 mg/kg), or JWZ-8-103 (50 mg/kg); an additional dilution was made using sterile 100 mmol/L potassium phosphate buffer and 32 mmol/L sucrose, pH 6.8, for JWZ-8-103 (15 mg/kg).

Investigators who provided treatment and monitored tumor growth were blinded to treatment designation. Tumor size was measured using an electronic caliper; then, volume values were plotted using GraphPad Prism version 10.

Introduction
Refractory pancreatic cancer remains one of the greatest challenges in oncology, with limited therapeutic options and poor patient outcomes (
1
). Developing new targeted therapies for this aggressive malignancy is imperative to improve survival rates. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of targeting “non-oncogene addiction,” a phenomenon in which cancer cells become dependent on specific proteins or pathways for survival and growth (
2
–
4
). One such emerging target is the nuclear pore complex (NPC), which is essential for the efficient transport of mRNAs, proteins, and metabolites between the nucleus and cytoplasm (
5
). Cancer cells, due to their heightened metabolic demands and stress adaptation mechanisms, exhibit a greater dependence on active nuclear flux and transport than normal cells (
6
). Understanding the mechanisms by which the NPC can be selectively targeted to induce cancer cell death is crucial for developing effective treatments for challenging malignancies.
Molecular glues, small molecules that induce cooperative protein–protein binding events (
7
–
9
), have transformed the treatment of hematologic malignancies (
10
,
11
) but have not yet been approved for common solid tumors despite early promise (
12
). Although their pharmacologic properties are desirable, molecular glues have historically been discovered serendipitously (
13
,
14
). Modern strategies to rationally design therapeutics with molecular glue mechanisms focus on the chemical modification of known glue compounds (
15
). Though a proven drug discovery strategy, this approach does not generally deliver fundamentally new molecular glue mechanisms. Meanwhile, multiple practice-changing drugs, including cyclosporine and thalidomide, entered the clinic before being recognized as molecular glues (
13
), suggesting that there may be an untapped pool of molecular glues in potent existing drugs with unknown mechanisms.
Recent advances in cell-based phenotypic screening (
16
,
17
) and functional genomics (
18
) provide strong motivation to revisit promising drug candidates with unknown mechanisms of action, with the hypothesis that some could be acting as molecular glue degraders through novel E3 ubiquitin ligases (
19
). For example, our systematic screening of existing drugs (
20
) against more than 500 barcoded cancer cell lines (
21
) uncovered multiple molecular glue mechanisms, including a compound that induces DDB1–CDK12 binding (
22
). The TRIM family of ubiquitylating enzymes represent an emerging drug target class with significant potential for targeted protein degradation in cancer therapy (
23
,
24
). Of these, TRIM21 (Ro52) is an attractive therapeutic target for reprogramming given its proven role in degrading diverse substrates via the “Trim-Away” system (
25
). TRIM21 binds and ubiquitylates antibody constant regions, resulting in the destruction of antibody-bound pathogens (
26
,
27
). To date, no known TRIM21-targeting small molecules have intentionally advanced to clinical development.
As part of our search for new anticancer mechanisms, we have determined the mechanism of PRLX-93936 (PRLX), a clinical-stage cancer drug candidate. Originally synthesized by Prolexys Pharmaceuticals as an improved analog of the ferroptosis inducer erastin (
28
,
29
), PRLX instead induced apoptosis (
30
), implying an unknown target and accompanying molecular mechanism (
Fig. 1A
). Despite the lack of target-based knowledge, PRLX advanced to phase I clinical trials; it was adequately tolerated and showed early efficacy against multiple myeloma (
31
). Development was subsequently discontinued with the closure of the company. In this study, we report that PRLX functions as a molecular glue, binding TRIM21 and redirecting it to the NPC. Starting from PRLX, medicinal chemistry efforts yielded a series of improved molecular glues with increased potency and robust anticancer activity
in vivo
. These findings establish TRIM21 molecular glues as candidate therapeutics for pancreatic cancer and underscore the value of reexamining clinical-stage compounds with unknown mechanisms to discover additional molecular glues within the existing pharmacopeia.

Results
TRIM21 Expression Predicts PRLX Sensitivity
To identify predictive molecular biomarkers of PRLX sensitivity, we used PRISM, a molecular barcoding and pooled screening method (
16
), to measure the viability of ∼900 cancer cell lines treated with varying doses of PRLX (
Fig. 1B
; Supplementary Table S1). PRLX and its parent compound, erastin, had distinct cytotoxicity profiles across cell lines, consistent with their inducing cell death via different mechanisms (
Fig. 1C
). The PRLX activity profile was most highly correlated with mRNA expression of
TRIM21
(
Fig. 1D
), with higher
TRIM21
transcript abundance predicting sensitivity to PRLX (Pearson’s
r
= −0.58;
P
< 0.001;
Fig. 1E
). In addition, lineage-specific enrichment was seen for the inhibition of pancreatic and head and neck cancer cell lines versus other cancer types (
Fig. 1F
). To validate the pooled screening results against individual models, we selected 11 cancer cell lines with high
TRIM21
mRNA expression and found that all were highly sensitive to PRLX upon individual testing (
Fig. 1G
; Supplementary Fig. S1A). By contrast, three cancer cell lines with low
TRIM21
expression levels did not respond to PRLX. Ectopic overexpression of TRIM21 was sufficient to convert PRLX-insensitive cell lines to responders (
Fig. 1H
; Supplementary Fig. S1B). Thus, TRIM21 expression is strongly associated with PRLX sensitivity in cancer cell line models and is a potential biomarker to guide clinical development.
TRIM21 Is Required for PRLX-Induced Cytotoxicity
To identify genes functionally required for the PRLX response, we conducted genome-scale CRISPR/Cas9 gene knockout (KO) and activation drug modifier screens in TRIM21-expressing cancer cells. PANC-1 human pancreatic cancer cells were transduced with the Brunello single-guide RNA (sgRNA) KO library and treated with PRLX, erastin, or DMSO (control) for 21 days (Supplementary Fig. S1C; Supplementary Table S2). Samples for sgRNA sequencing were collected every 3 to 4 days (
Fig. 1I
). For PRLX, the top rescue hit at all time points was
TRIM21
itself, demonstrating that
TRIM21
is indeed required for drug response (
P
< 0.05;
Fig. 1J
). Additional rescue hits for PRLX included mediators of IFN and NF-κB signaling, such as
IRF2
,
CHUK
,
IKBKG
, and
HCFC2
(
P
< 0.05). No strong rescue hits were shared between the PRLX and erastin treatments (Supplementary Fig. S1D), further showing the distinct mechanisms of action of these compounds.
Genome-wide loss-of-function screens can identify factors required for drug activity, but they may underestimate the effects of essential factors and those that are expressed at low levels. We therefore also conducted a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 activation screen in PANC-1 cells using the Calabrese library (Supplementary Fig. S1E; Supplementary Table S3). CRISPR activation guides targeting the
TRIM21
promoter were depleted after a 13-day exposure to PRLX (
Fig. 1K
), consistent with the observation that TRIM21 expression sensitizes cells to PRLX. RNA guides targeting
IRF2
and
IRF1
, both of which are transcription factors that drive TRIM21 expression, were also depleted (
P
< 0.05).
PRDM1
(BLIMP1), a transcriptional repressor and regulator of B- and T-cell differentiation (
32
), was identified as a mediator of resistance to PRLX. BLIMP1 has also been reported to oppose IRF1 activity (
33
).
To confirm the screening results, we disrupted
TRIM21
using CRISPR/Cas9 in three cell lines (TRIM21 KO; Supplementary Table S4). TRIM21 KO was tolerated in all tested cell lines, and
TRIM21
is not essential in any cell lines in the Cancer Dependency Map (
34
). TRIM21 KO cells were highly resistant to PRLX, shifting the IC
50
from ∼100 nmol/L to greater than 10 μmol/L, whereas erastin sensitivity was unchanged (
Fig. 1L
; Supplementary Fig. S1F and S1G).
TRIM21
reintroduction using a guide-resistant cDNA restored PRLX sensitivity (Supplementary Fig. S1H). RING E3 ligases, including TRIM21, rely on a critical “linchpin” residue, most commonly arginine, to catalyze the transfer of ubiquitin from an E2 enzyme to a substrate protein (
35
). Expression of the TRIM21-R55E linchpin mutant did not fully restore PRLX sensitivity in TRIM21 KO PANC-1 cells (Supplementary Fig. S1H). Thus, functionally proficient TRIM21 is required for PRLX-mediated cell toxicity. We also knocked out
IRF2
,
CHUK
,
IKBKG
, and
HCFC2
in PANC-1 cells (Supplementary Table S4). Like TRIM21, IRF2 KO rendered PRLX inactive (Supplementary Fig. S2A and S2B). The IRF2 transcription factor promotes IFN-mediated immune responses and, via this activity, also modulates cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis. We found that IRF2 is required for robust TRIM21 expression (Supplementary Fig. S2C and S2D), consistent with a previous report of direct transcriptional TRIM21 regulation (
36
). Thus, IRF2 likely modulates PRLX activity indirectly via
TRIM21
transcription. CHUK or IKBKG KO only partially prevented PRLX-induced cytotoxicity (Supplementary Fig. S2A and S2B). Both factors are key components of the IκB kinase complex essential for canonical NF-κB activation. Therefore, although PRLX treatment rapidly activated NF-κB and IFN signaling (Supplementary Fig. S3A–S3F; Supplementary Table S5), consistent with the known function of TRIM21 as an innate immune sensor, this activity does not fully explain the antiproliferative activity of the compound. Thus, unknown factor(s) are required for PRLX-induced cancer cell death. Collectively, our genetic analysis demonstrated that TRIM21 is essential for the cell killing effects of PRLX and identified transcriptional circuits and signaling pathways that regulate sensitivity.
Structure–Activity Relationship and Improved PRLX Analogs
TRIM21-dependent activity is a heretofore unknown feature of PRLX pharmacology, suggesting an opportunity to synthesize new, more potent analogs with the same mechanism of action. To pursue this idea, we synthesized a series of PRLX analogs and tested their cytotoxic activities in isogenic PANC-1 wild-type (WT) and TRIM21 KO cells (
Fig. 2A–C
). The parental compound consists of three modifiable regions: a quinazolinone core (region A), an attached piperazine ring (region B), and a nitrogen-linked ethyl phenyl ether (region C). Replacement of N1 in the quinazolin-4(3H)-one core with carbon yielded inactive compounds, indicating that the quinazolinone core scaffold is essential for potency (compound
3
). In contrast, introducing a fluoro substitution at the C6 position enhanced potency to 40 nmol/L in compound
4
. Introducing chloro or iodo substituents at the same position greatly decreased or abolished activity (compounds
5
,
6
). Similarly, methyl, methoxy, bromo, or iodo substituents added at the C7 or C8 positions weakened potency (compounds
7–10
), suggesting that the quinazolinone core (region A) interacts with a shallow hydrophobic pocket. Modifications to the piperazine ring (region B), such as nitrogen methylation or acetylation, significantly decreased activity (compounds
11
and
12
). Likewise, nitrogen substitution by oxygen eliminated activity, indicating a crucial terminal nitrogen interaction with the binding pocket (compound
13
). Bridged piperidine did not enhance the potency (compounds
14
and
15
). Elimination of the ethoxy group (region C) abrogated activity (compound
16
), as did relocating it from the ortho to the meta or para position (compounds
17
,
18
). Subtler modifications to the 2-ethoxy-phenyl group were tolerated; methyl, bromo, and chloro substituents installed at the para position of the phenyl ring enhanced potency by at least 2-fold. Conversely, modifications at the three, five, and six positions (compounds
22–27
), including the addition of halogens and trifluoromethyl groups, diminished the inhibitory activity. We combined the chemical modifications that most improved PRLX potency to synthesize JWZ-8-103 (compound
28
;
Fig. 2B
). JWZ-8-103 was 10-fold more potent than PRLX against parental PANC-1 (IC
50
= 9.5 nmol/L) and H661 cells overexpressing high levels of ectopic TRIM21 (IC
50
<10 nmol/L) while retaining TRIM21 dependence for its cytotoxic activity (
Fig. 2D
and
E
). PRISM large-scale cell line profiling further corroborated these findings, demonstrating improved potency for JWZ-8-103 while maintaining a strong correlation with PRLX (
Fig. 2F
).
TRIM21
mRNA expression remained the top predictive biomarker for JWZ-8-103 activity (
Fig. 2G
). Together, these results establish JWZ-8-103 as a highly optimized PRLX analog with improved potency and TRIM21-dependent cytotoxicity, laying a strong foundation for further mechanistic exploration and pharmacologic development.

PRLX and Related Analogs Directly Bind TRIM21
Based on the above results, we hypothesized that TRIM21 may be a direct molecular target of PRLX and our TRIM21-dependent PRLX analogs. Indeed, JWZ-8-103 treatment increased the thermal stability of TRIM21 by cellular thermal shift profiling (Supplementary Fig. S4A and S4B). To identify candidate surfaces for PRLX and PRLX analog binding to TRIM21, we used Cas9-mediated base editing for scanning mutagenesis in PANC-1 cells (Supplementary Fig. S5A and S5B; Supplementary Tables S6 and S7). We identified multiple drug-resistant TRIM21 alleles (D355, W383, and F450 in Supplementary Fig. S5C and S5D) and a high correlation between PRLX and JWZ-8-103 treatment conditions (Supplementary Fig. S5E). Resistance-conferring mutations clustered at three TRIM21 interfaces: (i) the RING domain binding site for ubiquitylating E2 enzymes, (ii) the central coiled-coil amino acids predicted to contact the TRIM21 PRYSPRY domain, and (iii) the antibody constant region binding site of the PRYSPRY domain (
Fig. 3A
and
B
). Disruption of interfaces (i) and (ii) likely ablates TRIM21 catalytic activity, thus suggesting interface (iii), which features a shallow hydrophobic pocket, as the most likely PRLX binding site.

To test this idea, we purified the TRIM21 PRYSPRY domain and used surface plasmon resonance (SPR) to measure compound binding (
Fig. 3C
; Supplementary Fig. S6A). PRLX and JWZ-8-103 bound the PRYSPRY domain, as judged by equilibrium response levels. JWZ-8-103 bound more strongly than PRLX, in agreement with their relative cellular potencies. JWZ-8-60 (compound
13
), which was inactive in cellular assays, bound only weakly. Thus, the TRIM21 antibody binding PRYSPRY domain is likely the cellular receptor for PRLX and its enhanced analogs.
To understand precisely how TRIM21 interacts with JWZ-8-103, we determined the crystal structure of the small molecule–TRIM21 PRYSPRY complex (Supplementary Table S8, PDB code: 9EK5). JWZ-8-103 binds to a shallow pocket (mentioned above) lined by hydrophobic amino acid side chains, including TRIM21-L370, TRIM21-W381, and TRIM21-W383 (
Fig. 3D
and
E
). Among the compound–protein interactions that drive SAR are hydrogen bonds between the terminal nitrogen of the JWZ-8-103 piperazine ring and the D355 side chain acid (
Fig. 3F
). TRIM21-F450 and TRIM21-W381 further coordinate the piperazine ring, and the terminal nitrogen of the piperazine moiety may form a cation–π interaction with these residues, further stabilizing this complex (
Fig. 3E
). Indeed, JWZ-8-60 (compound
13
), in which the terminal nitrogen is substituted by oxygen, is completely inactive and does not bind to TRIM21 by SPR. Observation of an ordered water coordinated by the D355 acid implies further space for chemical exploration. In addition to these interactions, the JWZ-8-103 chlorophenyl ring and its attached ortho-ethoxy group extend into a shallow hydrophobic patch defined by TRIM21-W383. TRIM21-L370, TRIM21-Y393, TRIM21-P394, and TRIM21-Q395 position the quinazoline-4(3H)-one core, enabling its near-complete desolvation. A buried hydrogen bond between the free pyrimidine nitrogen and the backbone amide hydrogen of L371 reinforces the position of the compound core. Substitution of this nitrogen by carbon in compound
3
ablates activity, consistent with this interpretation. Cellular point mutations underscored the importance of these contacts; TRIM21-D355A rendered PRLX and its analogs inactive, whereas TRIM21-W381A, TRIM21-W383A, and TRIM21-F450A also demonstrated reduced compound activity (
Fig. 3G
; Supplementary Fig. S6B). Thus, extensive hydrophobic and hydrogen bonding interactions mediate JWZ-8-103–TRIM21 binding despite the lack of a deep compound-binding cleft, as commonly seen for substrate-competitive enzyme inhibitors. Further interactions with TRIM21 neo-client proteins, as described below, likely further stabilize compound binding.
PRLX Induces TRIM21-Dependent Degradation of the NPC
The foregoing results suggested that PRLX and its analogs likely activate rather than inhibit TRIM21 function and could potentially redirect substrate recognition, as PRLX analogs bind to the substrate-recruiting surface of TRIM21. Accordingly, we hypothesized that unbiased proteomics would help identify candidate proteins in which degradation by TRIM21 was induced by PRLX (Supplementary Fig. S7A). We first measured time-dependent (30 minutes–10 hours) PRLX-induced changes in protein abundance in WT or TRIM21 KO PANC-1 cells (500 nmol/L PRLX for 6 hours; Supplementary Table S9). We observed rapid and deep TRIM21-dependent perturbation of the proteome in response to PRLX (
Fig. 4A
and
B
; Supplementary Fig. S7B–S7D). NPC proteins, especially nucleoporins (NUP) that are key building blocks, were overrepresented among depleted proteins with strong time dependence. By contrast, IRF and NF-κB pathway members exhibited more modest changes and only weak time dependence.

Upon individual review of NPC complex members, almost all structural components decreased in a time- and TRIM21-dependent manner (Supplementary Fig. S7E; EMB-14322 with PDB 7R5K). Cytoplasmic filament proteins (e.g., GLE1, NUP214, NUP88, AAAS, and RANBP2) and inner ring proteins (e.g., NUP155 and especially NUP35) were rapidly depleted. Immunoblotting confirmed these observations for representative NUPs (
Fig. 4C
). Furthermore, immunofluorescence microscopy demonstrated NPC loss at the single-cell level (Supplementary Fig. S7F). JWZ-8-103 (100 nmol/L) induced a very similar response proteome-wide as the PRLX parent compound, including downregulation of the antiapoptotic protein MCL1 (Supplementary Fig. S7G–S7I; ref.
37
). This is in stark contrast to the known mechanism of the PRLX precursor erastin, which induces ferroptosis by inhibiting the plasma membrane–localized system x
c
−
amino acid antiporter (
29
). Indeed, 10 μmol/L erastin (6 hours) had a minimal effect on the overall proteome of PANC-1 cells with or without TRIM21 present (Supplementary Fig. S7J and S7K). Instead, erastin induced the expression of GDF15, which is known to function as a mediator in erastin-induced ferroptosis (
38
).
Pretreatment with proteasome inhibitors (MG-132, bortezomib) or a ubiquitin-activating enzyme inhibitor (MLN-7243) prevented NUP degradation (Supplementary Fig. S8A), confirming active NUP clearance by the ubiquitin–proteasome system. To assess whether TRIM21 mediates ubiquitylation of the nuclear pore in PRLX-treated cells, we used diglycine remnant profiling to measure the ubiquitylated proteome in PANC-1 cells treated with 500 nmol/L PRLX (30 minutes; Supplementary Fig. S7A; Supplementary Table S10). NUPs depleted in global proteomics experiments were significantly ubiquitylated at one or more sites upon PRLX treatment (Supplementary Fig. S8B). MG132 pretreatment further improved quantification of PRLX-induced NUP ubiquitylation (e.g., GLE1, NUP88, NUP155;
Fig. 4D
).
We then employed proximity labeling proteomics (
39
) to determine whether PRLX induces TRIM21 trafficking to the nuclear pore. We expressed a TRIM21–TurboID fusion construct in PANC-1 TRIM21 KO cells and confirmed that PRLX exhibited TRIM21-dependent cytotoxicity across these model cell lines (Supplementary Fig. S8C). Next, we purified biotinylated proteins after PRLX treatment (500 nmol/L; 30 minutes or 2 hours; Supplementary Fig. S7A; Supplementary Table S11). NPC proteins were significantly enriched following PRLX treatment relative to two different controls: (i) DMSO supplemented with biotin and (ii) PRLX treatment (500 nmol/L for 2 hours) without biotin supplementation (
Fig. 4E
; Supplementary Fig. S8D–S8F). In this experiment, we also identified multiple E2 ubiquitination enzymes that interact with TRIM21, consistent with literature reports and in agreement with the genetic screens described above, in which knockout of any single E2 ligase did not strongly alter drug response (Supplementary Fig. S8E and S8F). Repeating the proximity labeling enrichment using immunoblotting visualization confirmed direct interactions with TRIM21 following PRLX treatment for key NUPs but not MCL1, consistent with our mass spectrometry (MS)–based proteomic profiling (
Fig. 4F
). Overrepresentation of the cytoplasmic filament (e.g., GLE1, NUP214, NUP88, etc.), central channel (e.g., NUP54, NUP58, NUP98), inner ring (e.g., NUP35 and NUP155), and coat (NUP133, NUP96, NUP107, SEC13) NUPs suggested TRIM21 recruitment to the cytoplasmic side of the inner ring (
Fig. 4G
and
H
). Collectively, our proteomic profiling studies indicate that PRLX binding redirects TRIM21 to the inner ring of the nuclear pore facing the cytoplasm, triggering ubiquitylation of nearby nuclear pore proteins and initiating subsequent proteasomal degradation.
NUP98 Recruits TRIM21-PRLX to the NPC

Discussion
Existing drugs with unknown mechanisms of action are a rich source of novel pharmacology. We present here an unexpected molecular glue degrader mechanism for the clinical-stage compound PRLX. An unbiased phenotypic screen revealed that PRLX activity was nearly exclusive to cells with high TRIM21 expression, which we confirmed through large-scale functional genomics. We used cellular assays to develop improved PRLX derivatives with greater potency and found the best of these to have robust anticancer activity
in vivo
. Our structural and biochemical studies, which were enabled by the more potent PRLX analog, demonstrated that the substrate binding domain of TRIM21 serves as the PRLX receptor. Through quantitative global proteome profiling, ubiquitin profiling, and proximity labeling proteomics, we discovered that the PRLX-TRIM21 complex binds and induces the degradation of nuclear pore proteins via the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway. Close examination of genetic data led us to reconstitute a molecular glue interaction between TRIM21-PRLX and the nuclear pore protein NUP98. Indeed, NUP98 binds TRIM21 only in the presence of the compound and has no discernible interaction with TRIM21 in untreated cells. Thus, PRLX and its more potent analogs catalyze a “friendly fire” effect by triggering the TRIM21 innate immune sensor to destroy an essential cellular structure in cancer cells.
Our findings complement recent work demonstrating that diverse molecules, including acepromazine metabolites, PRLX, and other compounds, can bind TRIM21 and, when bound, have molecular glue activity against the NPC (
51
–
54
). These collective insights strengthen the emerging perspective that TRIM21 and its relatives are druggable enzymes (
55
). Studying binding site homology between TRIM21 and other PRYSPRY domain–containing TRIMs could enable further compound optimization to recruit proteins with specialized functions or unique expression patterns.
Our potent TRIM21 molecular glue degraders provide a robust toolkit for future studies of acute perturbation of the NPC across cancer models and normal tissues. The NPC is the gatekeeper of nucleocytoplasmic transport and signaling, through which a vast flux of materials is continuously exchanged to maintain cellular homeostasis. Growing evidence suggests there may be an unexpectedly wide therapeutic index for targeting the nuclear pore in cancer cells (
6
). Potential contributors to this selectivity include (i) increased dependence of cancer cells on active nuclear transport (
56
), (ii) varying levels of apoptotic priming (
57
), and (iii) required ongoing nuclear import of key oncogenic transcription factors (
58
).
Our study highlights a potential therapeutic window for targeted NPC degradation in pancreatic cancer. Among more than 6,000 drugs tested against the PRISM cell line panel, PRLX ranks among the top 20 most cell line selective and predictable based on our published metrics (
21
). PRLX, when administered to patients in a clinical trial, proved tolerable up to 20 mg/m
2
(
31
), suggesting a viable path toward the clinical translation of our findings. However, it should be noted that although a maximum tolerated dose was established for PRLX, detailed human PK data have not been published. There remains a risk of on-mechanism toxicity due to NPC degradation in TRIM21-expressing healthy tissues. Several strategies should be employed to understand and mitigate risks associated with targeting essential proteins such as the NPC in patients with cancer (
59
), including biomarker-based patient stratification based on TRIM21 tumor expression, further target evaluation across multiple tissue types, and careful optimization of both drug dose and schedule. JWZ-8-103 will require formal investigational new drug-enabling toxicology studies prior to clinical trials. We note that the mouse TRIM21 sequence includes amino acid differences near the compound binding site revealed by our crystal structure. Therefore, future toxicology studies should incorporate higher-order species, potentially including nonhuman primates.
Employing a molecular glue degrader to target the nuclear pore has great potential pharmacologic advantages. Sustained NPC inactivation can occur at relatively low compound concentrations due to repeated cycles of target degradation, and these effects last long after the drug has been cleared from tissue. Indeed, PD markers of PRLX analog activity in tissue (nuclear pore protein degradation) outlasted the half-life of the drug itself in mouse studies. The development of future PRLX derivatives that retain TRIM21 binding and redirect its ubiquitylating activity toward other neosubstrates could potentially expand the scope of degradable proteins in cells for novel applications.
Given the substantial resources necessary for oncology clinical development, we recommend that cell line phenotypic profiling be performed with all anticancer small molecules during development to capture as much information as possible about their pharmacologic activities and candidate biomarkers. Our work demonstrates the power of unbiased phenotypic screening coupled with orthogonal approaches toward target identification, functional validation, and deciphering of the mechanism of action. The discovery of the PRLX mechanism of action through TRIM21-mediated degradation of nuclear pore proteins opens new avenues for targeted cancer therapy.

2
for 1/K

start, 1.30 V⋅s/cm
2
for 1/K

PK Study
The PK study was performed in the Drug Metabolism and Pharmacokinetics (DMPK) Core facility at Scripps Florida. PKs were tested in male C57BL/6 mice via intravenous dosing in the tail vein, i.p. injection, and oral gavage. Triplicate mice were dosed at 1 mg/kg intravenously, 3 mg/kg intraperitoneally, and 6 mg/kg orally, formulated at 0.2 mg/mL (intravenously), 0.3 mg/mL (intraperitoneally), and 0.6 mg/mL (orally) in a 5:5:90 DMSO/Tween80/water solution. Approximately 20 μL of blood was collected after 5, 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 360, and 480 minutes. We used a microsampling technique in which blood is collected in capillary hematocrit tubes to reduce the total blood taken from the mouse. This allowed a single mouse to be used for the entire time course and reduced interindividual variability. Additionally, by using small sample volumes, the health of the mouse is maintained. Plasma was generated by standard centrifugation techniques, yielding approximately 10 μL of plasma, which was immediately frozen. Plasma (5 μL) was treated with 75 μL of an 80:20 acetonitrile/water solution containing 20 ng/mL carbamazepine as an internal standard and allowed to sit on ice for approximately 30 minutes to precipitate plasma proteins. A standard curve ranging from 1 to 3,300 ng/mL was prepared in mouse plasma and processed with the samples. Samples were filtered through a 0.2-micron filter and directly analyzed. Drug concentrations were determined by mass spectrometry using an SCIEX 5500 mass spectrometer with multiple reaction monitoring, using the mass transition of 365.2 to 99 for PRLX and 418.2 to 99 for JWZ-8-103, and comparing the peak area with the area of the carbamazepine internal standard. PK parameters were calculated using a noncompartmental model (Phoenix WinNonlin, Pharsight Inc.). All procedures were approved by the Scripps Florida Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee, and the Scripps vivarium is fully accredited by the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care International.
